q: The dashed AS1 curve lies above the original AS0 curve. What change does this graph show?
options: A decrease in aggregate supply
An increase in aggregate supply
An increase in aggregate demand
A decrease in aggregate demand
feedback: When the aggregate supply curve shifts left/up, less output is supplied at each price level, which is a decrease in aggregate supply.

q: If the economy moves from AS0 to AS1 in the graph, what happens to real GDP and the price level?
options: Real GDP increases while the price level decreases
Real GDP decreases while the price level increases
Both real GDP and the price level increase
Both real GDP and the price level decrease
feedback: An inward/leftward AS shift reduces output and raises the price level.

q: Which event best matches the shift from AS0 to AS1?
options: Higher consumer confidence that boosts spending
A cut in income taxes that raises aggregate demand
A rise in input prices that makes production more costly
A fall in the overall price level causing a movement along AS0
feedback: Higher production costs shift short-run aggregate supply left.

q: At real GDP of 150, the price level on AS0 is 150 and the price level on AS1 is 190. By how much does the price level rise at that output level?
feedback: At the same output level, the price level increases from 150 to 190, a rise of 40.

q: A student says the graph shows a recession with inflation pressure occurring at the same time. Which label best fits that combination?
options: Stagflation caused by a negative aggregate supply shock
Demand-pull expansion caused by an AD increase
Long-run growth caused by a rise in LRAS
Deflation caused by an AD decrease
feedback: A leftward shift of AS reduces output and raises prices, the classic stagflation pattern.

q: Which statement best interprets the shift from AS0 to AS1 without confusing it for a movement along a curve?
options: At every price level, consumers demand more output than before, so aggregate demand has increased
At every real GDP level, producers now require a higher price level than before, so aggregate supply has decreased
The economy slides downward along AS0, so price level and output both fall
The graph shows LRAS moving right, so potential output rises while prices fall
feedback: The entire AS curve shifted up/left. That means production is less forthcoming at each price level, not that the economy merely moved to another point on AS0.

q: The dashed AD1 curve lies to the right of AD0. What change does the graph show?
options: A decrease in aggregate demand
An increase in aggregate supply
An increase in aggregate demand
A decrease in aggregate supply
feedback: A rightward shift of AD means aggregate demand has increased.

q: If the economy moves from AD0 to AD1 with aggregate supply held fixed, what happens to real GDP and the price level?
options: Real GDP decreases while the price level increases
Real GDP increases while the price level decreases
Both real GDP and the price level decrease
Both real GDP and the price level increase
feedback: A rightward shift of AD raises spending pressure, so equilibrium output and the price level both rise in the short run.

q: Which event is most consistent with the shift from AD0 to AD1?
options: An increase in consumer, investment, government, or net-export spending
A rise in input costs that shifts AS left
An increase in wages that reduces aggregate supply
A fall in productivity that lowers long-run output
feedback: Aggregate demand shifts right when planned spending rises.

q: At a price level of 50, the graph shows real GDP of 100 on AD0 and 150 on AD1. By how much does quantity of real GDP demanded increase?
feedback: At price level 50, the quantity of output demanded rises from 100 to 150, an increase of 50.

q: A student says AD1 must represent aggregate supply because real GDP is larger. What is the best correction?
options: Any curve farther right must always be aggregate supply
The graph is actually showing LRAS because real GDP is on the horizontal axis
AD is the downward-sloping spending curve, so a rightward shift from AD0 to AD1 still represents aggregate demand, not aggregate supply
Because price level is measured vertically, the curve cannot represent demand
feedback: The label and downward slope identify the curves as AD. A larger quantity demanded at each price level is an increase in aggregate demand.

q: Which statement correctly interprets the move from AD0 to AD1?
options: At each real GDP level, firms are willing to produce more because input costs fell
The economy experiences a movement upward along the same AD curve due to inflation alone
Potential output rises because LRAS shifts right with no change in spending
At each price level, households, firms, government, and foreigners together demand more real output than before
feedback: An AD increase means spending is higher at every price level. That is a shift of the entire demand curve, not a movement along it.

q: The dashed AD1 curve lies to the left of AD0. What change does the graph show?
options: A decrease in aggregate demand
An increase in aggregate demand
An increase in aggregate supply
A decrease in aggregate supply
feedback: A leftward shift of AD means aggregate demand has decreased.

q: If the economy moves from AD0 to AD1 with aggregate supply held fixed, what happens to real GDP and the price level?
options: Real GDP increases while the price level decreases
Both real GDP and the price level decrease
Real GDP decreases while the price level increases
Both real GDP and the price level increase
feedback: A leftward shift of AD lowers spending pressure, reducing equilibrium output and the price level in the short run.

q: Which event best matches the shift from AD0 to AD1?
options: A productivity improvement that shifts AS right
A fall in input costs that increases aggregate supply
A fall in planned spending such as lower consumption or investment
A higher expected price level that moves the economy along AS
feedback: Lower overall spending shifts aggregate demand left.

q: At a price level of 45, the graph shows real GDP of 150 on AD0 and 100 on AD1. By how much does quantity of real GDP demanded fall?
feedback: At price level 45, quantity demanded falls from 150 to 100, a decrease of 50.

q: A policymaker wants to reverse the move from AD0 to AD1. Which macro pattern is the policymaker trying to avoid?
options: A drop in output accompanied by downward pressure on the price level
A rise in output accompanied by inflationary pressure from excess spending
A rise in output from improved productivity
A higher price level paired with a fall in output from a negative supply shock
feedback: A decrease in AD lowers both real GDP and the price level in the short run.

q: Which statement best captures the meaning of the shift from AD0 to AD1?
options: At every real GDP level, firms must be paid a lower price level, so aggregate supply has increased
At every price level, the total quantity of real output demanded is lower than before, so aggregate demand has decreased
The graph shows a movement along AD0 caused only by a lower price level
Potential output falls because LRAS shifts left even though demand stays constant
feedback: The entire AD curve shifts left. That means spending is lower at each price level, not that the economy merely moved along AD0.

q: The dashed AS1 curve lies below the original AS0 curve. What change does this graph show?
options: A decrease in aggregate supply
An increase in aggregate demand
An increase in aggregate supply
A decrease in aggregate demand
feedback: A downward/rightward shift of the AS curve means aggregate supply has increased.

q: If the economy moves from AS0 to AS1 with aggregate demand held fixed, what happens to real GDP and the price level?
options: Real GDP decreases while the price level increases
Both real GDP and the price level increase
Both real GDP and the price level decrease
Real GDP increases while the price level decreases
feedback: A rightward shift of AS increases output and lowers the price level.

q: Which event best matches the shift from AS0 to AS1?
options: A fall in input costs or an improvement in productivity
A surge in household spending
An increase in government purchases that shifts AD right
A rise in inflation expectations that shifts SRAS left
feedback: Lower costs or better productivity shift aggregate supply right.

q: At real GDP of 150, the price level on AS0 is 150 and the price level on AS1 is 110. By how much does the price level fall at that output level?
feedback: At the same output level, price level falls from 150 to 110, a decrease of 40.

q: A student claims the graph shows demand-pull growth. What is the strongest correction?
options: The graph shows a rightward shift of aggregate demand, which raises both price level and output
The graph shows LRAS shifting left, which lowers output and raises prices
The graph shows a rightward shift of aggregate supply, which lowers the price level while raising output
The graph shows no shift at all, only a movement along AS0
feedback: Demand-pull expansions raise both price level and output. This graph instead shows more output paired with a lower price level, which is an AS increase.

q: Which statement best interprets the move from AS0 to AS1?
options: At every price level, buyers demand less output than before, so aggregate demand has fallen
The economy moves upward along AS0 because input prices increased
Potential output is unchanged because no supply-side forces are involved
At every real GDP level, producers are willing to supply output at a lower price level than before, so aggregate supply has increased
feedback: A lower AS curve means firms will supply more at each price level, or the same output at a lower price level. That is an increase in aggregate supply.

q: In the AD-AS-LRAS graph, which labeled point represents the original long-run equilibrium before aggregate demand increases?
options: Point C
Point A
Point B
Point D
feedback: The original long-run equilibrium is where AD0, SRAS0, and LRAS0 meet. That is point C.

q: If aggregate demand increases from AD0 to AD1 while SRAS0 is still fixed in the short run, which point shows the short-run equilibrium?
options: Point A
Point D
Point B
Point C
feedback: With AD1 and SRAS0, the short-run equilibrium is point D.

q: After wages and expectations adjust, SRAS shifts from SRAS0 to SRAS1. Which point shows the new long-run equilibrium?
options: Point A
Point C
Point B
Point D
feedback: The new long-run equilibrium occurs where AD1, SRAS1, and LRAS0 intersect: point B.

q: Which sequence correctly traces the economy after an increase in aggregate demand starting from the original long-run equilibrium?
options: C to A to D
A to C to B
D to C to A
C to D to B
feedback: The economy begins at C, moves to D in the short run when AD increases, and returns to long-run output at B after SRAS shifts left.

q: Comparing the original long-run equilibrium C with the new long-run equilibrium B, what is true?
options: Real GDP returns to 100 while the price level rises from 125 to 175
Real GDP rises to 125 while the price level remains 125
Real GDP falls to 75 while the price level remains 150
Real GDP stays 100 while the price level falls from 125 to 100
feedback: LRAS stays at 100, so long-run real GDP returns to 100. The long-run price level is higher at B than at C.

q: A student says an aggregate-demand increase permanently raises real GDP above potential in this graph. Which correction is best?
options: It never changes price level, because LRAS determines only inflation
It raises real GDP above potential only in the short run at D; after SRAS shifts left, the economy returns to potential output at B with a higher price level
It permanently moves the economy to D because SRAS does not adjust
It lowers real GDP below potential in the short run and restores it at A
feedback: The graph shows short-run output above LRAS at D, but long-run adjustment returns output to LRAS at B while price level stays higher.

q: Which labeled point is the original long-run equilibrium in the graph with LRAS0 and LRAS1?
options: Point B
LRAS1
Point A
SRAS1
feedback: Point A is where AD0, SRAS0, and LRAS0 intersect.

q: Which labeled point is the new long-run equilibrium after the supply-side improvement?
options: Point A
LRAS0
SRAS0
Point B
feedback: Point B is where AD0, SRAS1, and LRAS1 intersect.

q: From point A to point B, what happens to real GDP and the price level?
options: Real GDP rises from 100 to 115 while the price level falls from 125 to 110
Real GDP falls from 115 to 100 while the price level rises from 110 to 125
Both real GDP and the price level rise
Both real GDP and the price level fall
feedback: The graph shows more long-run output and a lower price level at the new equilibrium.

q: Which event best matches the joint shift from SRAS0/LRAS0 to SRAS1/LRAS1?
options: A drop in consumer confidence that reduces aggregate demand
A productivity improvement that raises potential output and lowers production costs
A rise in energy prices that lowers aggregate supply
An increase in government spending that shifts AD right
feedback: A positive supply-side change can shift both SRAS right and LRAS right.

q: Which statement best describes the macro outcome shown by the move from A to B?
options: The economy experiences recession with accelerating inflation
The economy shows pure demand-pull inflation with no growth
The economy experiences long-run growth with disinflationary pressure
The economy remains stuck at the same output and price level
feedback: Higher LRAS and SRAS support more output alongside a lower price level.

q: A student says point B can only be explained by higher aggregate demand because real GDP is larger there. Which correction best fits the graph?
options: Point B is created by a rightward shift of AD with no supply changes, so the student is correct
Point B is created by a leftward shift of SRAS, which raises output and lowers prices
Point B is impossible because LRAS cannot move in macroeconomics
Point B is created by rightward shifts of both SRAS and LRAS while AD stays at AD0, so higher output comes from stronger supply, not stronger demand
feedback: The graph holds AD constant and shows the supply side improving. That raises potential output and lowers the price level.

q: In the AD-AS graph, which point shows the original equilibrium before aggregate demand rises?
options: Point A
Point B
AD1
AS0
feedback: Point A is the intersection of AD0 and AS0.

q: After aggregate demand shifts from AD0 to AD1 while AS0 is fixed, which point shows the new short-run equilibrium?
options: Point A
Point B
AD0
AS1
feedback: Point B is where AD1 intersects AS0.

q: From point A to point B, by how much does real GDP increase?
feedback: Real GDP rises from 150 to 175, an increase of 25.

q: From point A to point B, by how much does the price level increase?
feedback: The price level rises from 125 to 137.5, an increase of 12.5.

q: Which description best matches the move from A to B?
options: The economy moves upward along a fixed AS0 curve because aggregate demand increases
The AS curve shifts right while aggregate demand stays constant
The economy moves downward along AD0 because aggregate supply decreases
Both AD and AS shift so the economy returns to its original output
feedback: With AS0 unchanged, the AD increase causes a movement along the AS curve to a new short-run equilibrium.

q: A student sees higher output and a higher price level at point B and concludes the graph must show an aggregate-supply increase. What is the best correction?
options: An aggregate-supply increase always raises both output and the price level, so the student is correct
An aggregate-supply increase would raise output but lower the price level; this graph shows both rising, which is the short-run signature of an aggregate-demand increase
A demand increase would lower output and raise the price level, so this cannot be AD
Because the graph lacks LRAS, no conclusion about demand or supply is possible
feedback: In a standard AD-AS model, a rightward AD shift raises both output and prices in the short run, unlike a rightward AS shift.

q: Which point marks the original equilibrium where AD0 and AS0 intersect?
options: Point B
Point C
Point A
Point D
feedback: Point A is the initial intersection of AD0 and AS0.

q: If only aggregate demand increases from AD0 to AD1 while AS0 stays in place, which point shows the new equilibrium?
options: Point A
Point C
Point D
Point B
feedback: With AD1 and AS0, the equilibrium is point B.

q: If only aggregate supply decreases from AS0 to AS1 while AD0 stays in place, which point shows the new equilibrium?
options: Point D
Point A
Point B
Point C
feedback: With AD0 and AS1, the equilibrium is point D.

q: If aggregate demand increases from AD0 to AD1 at the same time aggregate supply decreases from AS0 to AS1, which point shows the resulting equilibrium?
options: Point A
Point C
Point B
Point D
feedback: The simultaneous changes place the economy at the intersection of AD1 and AS1, which is point C.

q: Compare point A with point C. Which statement is correct?
options: Real GDP rises from 75 to 100 while the price level stays at 100
Real GDP falls from 75 to 50 while the price level stays at 125
Real GDP is unchanged at 75, but the price level rises from 100 to 150
Real GDP is unchanged at 75 and the price level falls from 150 to 100
feedback: The AD increase and AS decrease offset each other in output but reinforce each other on the price level.

q: A student says the graph proves output must rise whenever aggregate demand increases. Which graph-based rebuttal is strongest?
options: Yes, because point B shows that every AD increase always raises output no matter what happens to supply
No, because an AD increase always lowers the price level when supply shifts left
Yes, because simultaneous shifts cannot be analyzed with AD-AS graphs
Not if aggregate supply falls at the same time: moving from A to C leaves real GDP unchanged at 75 while the price level rises sharply to 150
feedback: Point B isolates the AD increase and point D isolates the AS decrease. Point C shows their combination, where the output effect is offset but inflation is amplified.
